lessons.title: Securing databases
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a cylinder-shaped database surrounded by a padlock, with a magnifying glass watching the queries and three small windows that each show only part of the data.
objectives: Apply least privilege to the accounts and applications that access a database.
Use views, stored procedures and encryption to limit exposure.
Monitor the activity of a database.

references.title: CIS Benchmarks for database management systems

blocks.text: The database, a priority target

Databases concentrate the most valuable information: customers, payroll, health, trade secrets. An attacker almost always tries to reach them. Protecting them combines access control, hardening, encryption, backups and monitoring.

rows: Everyone accesses only what they must
The application reads orders, without administration rights
Show only some of the columns or rows
Support sees the customer's name, not their IBAN
"create_order" instead of direct access to the tables
Transparent data encryption (TDE), encrypted "card number" column
See and alert on suspicious queries
Default accounts removed, database not exposed to the Internet

blocks.title: View, database (vue)
blocks.text: Virtual table built by a query, which presents only part of the data. Granting access to a view rather than to the table applies least privilege.
Three threats specific to databases

blocks.title: Aggregation, inference and their countermeasure
blocks.alt: Four-cell table: aggregation combines low-sensitivity data to obtain sensitive information; inference deduces hidden information from accessible data; polyinstantiation presents different versions according to clearance level; context control limits combinations of queries.

blocks.title: Aggregation (agrégation)
blocks.text: Combination of several low-sensitivity pieces of data that, put together, reveal sensitive information. Example: the delivery addresses and order dates of a military supplier reveal the movements of a unit.

blocks.title: Inference (inférence)
blocks.text: Deduction of information you have no access to from data you do have access to. Example: the total payroll of a two-person department and the salary of one of them reveal the salary of the other.

blocks.title: Polyinstantiation
blocks.text: Polyinstantiation means keeping several versions of the same record according to clearance level. An uncleared user sees a harmless version ("ship on exercise") instead of a refusal that would betray the existence of secret information. It is a countermeasure to inference.
Aggregation = add up to know. Inference = deduce to know. Polyinstantiation = show another version to hide that there is a secret.
Transaction integrity

rows: All or nothing: a transaction is either fully done or fully canceled
The database moves from one valid state to another valid state
Simultaneous transactions do not interfere with each other
A committed transaction survives a failure

blocks.text: Questions on aggregation and inference look alike. Ask yourself: is the person gathering a lot of data (aggregation) or reasoning from a few pieces (inference)? And remember that polyinstantiation answers inference.

blocks.title: SOC case: a nighttime extraction
blocks.text: On a demonstration database, the activity monitoring tool (DAM) raises an alert: at 3 a.m., the website's service account runs a "SELECT *" query on the whole customer table, whereas it usually reads only one order at a time. The analyst disables the account, discovers an SQL injection in a form, and the team restricts the account to stored procedures.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Database administrator: I remove default accounts and separate administration accounts from application accounts.
SOC analyst: a query that returns thousands of rows at once deserves an alert.
Auditor: I check who has administration rights and whether access to sensitive data is logged.
CISO: sensitive databases are never exposed directly to the Internet.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Aggregation ≠ inference: gathering or deducing.
Polyinstantiation is a countermeasure to inference.
Views limit what a user sees: least privilege.
ACID = atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability.
Least privilege, views, stored procedures, encryption, hardening, monitoring (DAM).
Aggregation: gathering harmless data; inference: deducing hidden data.
Polyinstantiation: one version per clearance level.
ACID guarantees transaction integrity.

lessons.title: Classifying data and managing its life cycle
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of three folders with colored labels: green public, yellow internal, red confidential, and a circular arrow going from creation to destruction.
objectives: Classify data according to its sensitivity.
Tell apart the roles: owner, custodian, user, controller and processor.
Describe the data life cycle, from creation to destruction.
Protect data in its three states: at rest, in transit, in use.

blocks.text: Why classify?

You cannot protect everything at the same level: it would be too expensive and too restrictive. Classification indicates the value and sensitivity of each piece of information, so the right measures can be applied to it: encryption, access, retention, destruction.

In the public and military sectors, other scales are found, for example: Unclassified, Confidential, Secret, Top Secret. The principle is the same: the more severe the impact of a disclosure, the higher the level.

blocks.title: The owner classifies
blocks.text: The data owner (a business manager) decides on its classification and on who can access it. The custodian (often the IT team) applies the protections day to day: backups, rights, encryption. Security advises, but does not classify in place of the business.
The roles

rows: Classifies, decides on access, is accountable for protection
Implements the protections: backups, rights, encryption
Uses the data according to the rules
Determines the purposes and means of processing personal data
Processes personal data on behalf of the controller
Advises on and monitors GDPR compliance

blocks.text: The life cycle

blocks.title: From creation to destruction
blocks.alt: Six-stage cycle: create, store, use, share, archive, destroy, then back to the creation of new data.

rows: Access control, isolation, confidential computing enclaves

blocks.text: Three states: at rest (disk), in transit (network), in use (memory). Each has its own protection.

Remember the difference in vocabulary: owner = responsibility and decision; custodian = technical implementation. A question asking "who decides on the classification" expects the owner, never the administrator.

blocks.title: SOC case: a mislabeled file
blocks.text: In an exercise, a payroll spreadsheet labeled "Internal" is sent to a contractor. The data loss prevention tool does not block it, because it relies on the label. The investigation shows that the file had been created from an "Internal" template. The payroll owner reclassifies the template as "Confidential" and a rule now detects social security numbers whatever the labeling.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Business owner: I decide who needs my data and for how long.
Administrator (custodian): I apply the rights and check the backups.
Auditor: I check that every piece of sensitive data has an owner and a retention period.
DPO: I make sure that personal data has a purpose and a legal basis.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: The owner classifies; the custodian protects.
Data must be protected in all three states, not only at rest.
A classification is reviewed: information can become public (for example after an announcement).
Controller = decides; processor = carries out on its behalf.
Classify according to the impact of disclosure; label and protect accordingly.
Owner, custodian, user; controller, processor, DPO.
Life cycle: create, store, use, share, archive, destroy.
Three states: at rest, in transit, in use.

lessons.title: Preventing leaks and destroying data
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a hard drive going into a shredder, next to a document in which some digits are hidden by asterisks.
objectives: Explain the role of a data loss prevention (DLP) solution.
Tell apart masking, tokenization, pseudonymization and anonymization.
Choose a suitable erasure method: clear, purge, destroy.
Apply the main GDPR principles to personal data.

references.title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Media Sanitization (2025)

blocks.text: Preventing leaks (DLP)

blocks.title: DLP, data loss prevention (prévention des fuites de données)
blocks.text: Set of tools and rules that spot sensitive data (by its content or its label) and prevent or report its unauthorized exit: email, USB drive, cloud, printing.

rows: Copying to a USB drive, printing, uploading
Public shares, SaaS applications (often through a CASB)

blocks.text: Reducing data exposure

blocks.title: Four techniques, four levels of reversibility
blocks.alt: Four-cell table: masking hides part of a piece of data on display; tokenization replaces the data with a token, reversible through a vault; pseudonymization replaces the identity but remains personal data; anonymization makes re-identification impossible and falls outside the scope of the GDPR.

cells.label: Pseudonymization
cells.detail: reversible with a key: GDPR applies

blocks.title: Pseudonymizing is not anonymizing
blocks.text: Pseudonymized data (the name replaced by an identifier, with a lookup table) remains personal data: the GDPR applies. Only truly anonymized data, from which nobody can re-identify the person, falls outside the scope of the GDPR. Anonymization is difficult: cross-referencing several datasets is often enough to re-identify.
Erasing for good
Deleting a file or formatting a disk does not erase the data: it remains readable with recovery tools. This is data remanence. NIST SP 800-88 distinguishes three levels of media sanitization.

rows: Overwriting of the data by software
Disk secure erase command, cryptographic erase, degaussing
The media can no longer be used

blocks.title: Crypto-shredding, cryptographic erase (effacement cryptographique)
blocks.text: Destruction of the key that encrypted data: without the key, the encrypted data becomes unreadable. Very useful in the cloud, where physical disks cannot be destroyed.

blocks.title: Degaussing and SSDs
blocks.text: Degaussing erases magnetic media such as traditional hard drives and tapes, but it is ineffective on SSDs and USB drives, which store data in flash memory. For them, use the manufacturer's secure erase, cryptographic erase or physical destruction.
Personal data: the essentials of the GDPR

blocks.title: Principles to apply
items: Lawfulness, fairness, transparency: a legal basis and clear information for individuals.
Purpose limitation: collect for a specific purpose.
Data minimization: collect only what is necessary.
Accuracy and storage limitation: up-to-date data, kept as long as necessary.
Integrity and confidentiality: appropriate security measures.
Data breach: notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless the risk to individuals is unlikely.

blocks.text: GDPR: "Less, for less time, better protected": minimize, limit retention, secure.

For destruction questions, look at two clues: the type of media (magnetic or flash) and what happens to the media (reused internally, resold, thrown away). The further the media leaves your control, the stronger the method must be.

blocks.title: SOC case: resold disks
blocks.text: During a simulated audit, a batch of decommissioned computers sold to a recycler is tested: on two disks that had simply been formatted, customer files are recovered in a few minutes. The SOC opens an incident, the DPO assesses whether notification is needed, and the procedure now requires a certified purge, with an erasure certificate for each disk.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: DPO: I prefer data that was never collected: minimization is the best protection.
SOC analyst: a DLP alert on a mass transfer to a personal mailbox has priority.
Auditor: I ask for the erasure certificates of decommissioned media.
CISO: in the cloud, I rely on encryption with my own keys and on cryptographic erase.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Formatting or deleting ≠ erasing: remanence.
Degaussing is ineffective on SSDs and flash memory.
Pseudonymization = still personal data.
GDPR notification to the authority: 72 hours.
DLP on the workstation, the network and the cloud.
Masking, tokenization, pseudonymization (reversible), anonymization (irreversible).
NIST SP 800-88: clear, purge, destroy; cryptographic erase.
GDPR: minimization, storage limitation, security, notification within 72 hours.

questions.prompt: Customer service must see customers' names but not their bank account numbers (IBAN). Which database feature fits?
choices: A view that exposes only the columns needed
An index on the customer name column
A daily backup of the customer table
Full access to the table, with a confidentiality reminder
questions.explanation: The view shows only part of the data: this is least privilege applied to the database.

whyNot.1: An index speeds up searches; it restricts nothing.
whyNot.2: The backup does not limit access.

questions.prompt: An employee gathers the delivery dates and addresses of many orders, none of them very sensitive, and deduces the movements of a military unit. What is this risk called?
choices: Replication
Aggregation
Normalization
Polyinstantiation
questions.explanation: Combining a lot of harmless data to obtain sensitive information is aggregation.

questions.prompt: What does the atomicity of a transaction guarantee?
choices: That it is anonymous and leaves no trace
That it is encrypted end to end
That it always runs in less than a second
That it is either fully completed or fully canceled
questions.explanation: All or nothing: a transfer cannot debit one account without crediting the other.

questions.prompt: A user knows the total payroll of a two-person department and the salary of one of them. They deduce the salary of the other. What is this?
choices: Inference
Aggregation
Privilege escalation
SQL injection
questions.explanation: They deduce information they do not have access to from accessible data: this is inference.

whyNot.1: They do not gather a large amount of data; they reason.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism shows an uncleared user a harmless version of a secret record, so that they cannot guess a secret exists?
choices: Differential backup
Hashing
Polyinstantiation
Aggregation
questions.explanation: Several versions of a record depending on the clearance level: it is a countermeasure against inference.

questions.prompt: Why give an application the right to run stored procedures rather than direct access to the tables?
choices: To remove the table access logs
So that it can only perform the intended operations
To avoid encrypting sensitive data
To speed up database backups
questions.explanation: Procedures limit the possible operations and reduce the impact of an application compromise.

questions.prompt: Which tool raises an alert when an application account reads the entire customer table at once at 3 a.m.?
choices: The stateful firewall placed in front of the server
Database activity monitoring (DAM)
Network address translation (NAT)
The nightly incremental backup
questions.explanation: DAM watches the queries and spots unusual behavior on the data.

whyNot.0: It sees connections, not the content of the queries.

questions.prompt: Which measures harden a production database? (several answers)
choices: Exposing the database port on the Internet for support
Separating administration accounts from application accounts
Encrypting the files and backups
Removing default accounts
questions.explanation: Removing default accounts, separating accounts and encryption greatly reduce the risk.

whyNot.0: A database must never be exposed directly on the Internet.

questions.prompt: Which measure best reduces the risk of inference in a salary statistics database?
choices: Increasing the size of the server's disks
Adding indexes on the salary columns
Refusing queries that cover groups that are too small
Disabling backups of the statistics database
questions.explanation: For a group of one or two people, a statistic reveals individual data: a minimum group size is set.

questions.prompt: The account a website uses to read orders must have:
choices: Database administrator rights
No password
Only the rights needed for its operations
The same password as the administrator
questions.explanation: If the site is compromised, the attacker will only have these limited rights.

whyNot.0: A compromise of the site would give away the whole database.

questions.prompt: Who decides on the classification of data?
choices: The system administrator who manages the server
The data owner (business manager)
The cloud provider that hosts the data
Any user who creates the data
questions.explanation: The owner knows the value of the data and is accountable for it; the custodian applies the protections.

whyNot.0: That is the custodian: they implement.
whyNot.2: The provider does not know the business value.

questions.prompt: TLS encryption protects data in which state?
choices: In use
At rest
In transit
Archived
questions.explanation: TLS encrypts data traveling over the network.

whyNot.1: At rest, disks and databases are encrypted.

questions.prompt: Which role implements the backups, rights and encryption decided for the data?
choices: The data owner
The custodian
The internal auditor
The data protection officer (DPO)
questions.explanation: The custodian applies, day to day, the protections decided by the owner.

whyNot.3: The DPO advises and monitors GDPR compliance.

questions.prompt: Why classify data?
choices: To automatically delete the oldest data
To encrypt all data at the same level, without exception
To speed up the network by reducing the volume of exchanges
To protect each piece of information according to its sensitivity
questions.explanation: Classification avoids overprotecting what is harmless and underprotecting what is sensitive.

whyNot.0: Destruction follows retention, not just age.
whyNot.1: Protecting everything to the maximum is costly and burdensome.

questions.prompt: A company entrusts its payroll to a service provider that processes employee data according to its instructions. What is the provider's role under the GDPR?
choices: Controller
Processor
Data protection officer
Supervisory authority
questions.explanation: The processor handles personal data on behalf of the controller, which sets the purposes.

whyNot.0: It is the company that sets the purposes.
whyNot.3: The supervisory authority is a public body (for example the CNIL in France).

questions.prompt: When should data be classified?
choices: Only in the event of an incident
Only when archiving
As soon as it is created
Never, it is pointless
questions.explanation: Classification guides all the following stages: storage, sharing, retention, destruction.

whyNot.1: Too late: it will have circulated without suitable protection.

questions.prompt: Financial results are "confidential" until their official publication. What should be done after publication?
choices: Destroy them immediately after publication
Leave them "confidential" forever, to be safe
Review their classification, for example to "public"
Encrypt them a second time with a new key
questions.explanation: Classification is reviewed: information loses its sensitivity when it becomes public.

whyNot.0: They may need to be retained.
whyNot.1: Needless overprotection is costly and burdensome.

questions.prompt: Which protection specifically targets data in use, in memory?
choices: Offline backup of the processed data
Confidential computing enclaves
TLS 1.3 on every connection to the server
Full-disk encryption of the server
questions.explanation: Enclaves protect data while it is being processed, even from the host system.

questions.prompt: The owner of a customer database is away and the administrator receives an access request from a new department. What should the administrator do?
choices: Grant access, since they have the technical ability and the rights
Permanently refuse any request from a new department
Copy the database into a new space reserved for the new department
Obtain the approval of the owner (or their designated deputy) before granting access
questions.explanation: The access decision belongs to the owner; the administrator (custodian) implements it.

questions.prompt: Which pairings between a protection and a data state are correct? (several answers)
choices: Memory isolation: data in use
VPN: data in transit
Disk encryption: data at rest
TLS: data at rest
questions.explanation: At rest: disk; in transit: network; in use: memory.

questions.prompt: Which tool can prevent a file containing credit card numbers from being sent by email?
choices: The company's internal DNS server
The stateful firewall of the mail gateway
The TPM module of the sender's workstation
DLP (data loss prevention)
questions.explanation: DLP recognizes sensitive data in the content and blocks or reports it leaving.

whyNot.1: It does not read the content of emails.
whyNot.2: The TPM protects keys on the machine.

questions.prompt: A disk is simply formatted before being given to a charity. What risk remains?
choices: The data can be recovered: data remanence
The disk can never be used again
The disk will be automatically encrypted by the system
None, because formatting permanently erases all the content
questions.explanation: Formatting erases the indexes, not the data: simple tools can recover it.

questions.prompt: Which GDPR principle requires collecting only the data that is needed?
choices: Data minimization
Aggregation
Polyinstantiation
Portability
questions.explanation: Minimizing reduces the impact of a leak: you cannot lose what you do not have.

whyNot.3: Portability is a right of individuals.

questions.prompt: Data in which the name is replaced by an identifier, with a mapping table kept separately: is it still subject to the GDPR?
choices: Only if it is printed or sent by email
No, it has become anonymous and falls outside the GDPR
No, provided that the mapping table is encrypted
Yes, it is pseudonymized data, and therefore still personal
questions.explanation: Re-identification remains possible with the table: the GDPR still applies.

whyNot.1: Anonymous would mean that nobody can re-identify.
whyNot.2: Encrypting the table does not change the nature of the data.

questions.prompt: Why is degaussing not suitable for an SSD?
choices: Because the GDPR prohibits it for personal data
Because an SSD uses flash memory, not magnetic media
Because it is too slow for high-capacity disks
Because it encrypts the disk instead of erasing the data
questions.explanation: For an SSD: the manufacturer's secure erase, cryptographic erasure or physical destruction.

whyNot.0: The GDPR does not prohibit a method.

questions.prompt: How can data stored at a cloud provider, whose disks cannot be destroyed, be made unreadable?
choices: Rename the files so that they are no longer recognized
Destroy the encryption key of that data (cryptographic erasure)
Deactivate the cloud account without deleting anything
Ask the provider to send over the physical disks
questions.explanation: Without the key, the encrypted data is unusable: this is cryptographic erasure.

whyNot.0: Renaming does not change the content.
whyNot.2: The data would remain in place.
whyNot.3: Rarely possible in a multi-tenant cloud.

questions.prompt: What is the tokenization of a credit card number?
choices: Full-disk encryption of the server that stores the numbers
Permanently deleting the number from all the company's databases
Replacing the number with a worthless token, with the mapping kept in a secure vault
Displaying only the last four digits, with the others masked on screen
questions.explanation: The systems that handle the token no longer need to see the real number, which reduces their exposure.

whyNot.1: Tokenization is reversible through the vault.

questions.prompt: Magnetic hard drives containing "secret" data are being retired and will not be reused. Which method is the most appropriate?
choices: Physical destruction (shredding), after purging if possible, with a certificate
Deleting the files and then emptying the recycle bin
Renaming the partitions and reinstalling the system
A simple quick format of each disk
questions.explanation: For a high classification level and media that will not be reused, destruction offers the best assurance.

questions.prompt: A customer database has been stolen and poses a risk to individuals. Under the GDPR, within what time frame must the supervisory authority be notified?
choices: The GDPR does not require any notification to the authority
72 hours after becoming aware of it, where feasible
30 days after discovery, once the investigation is complete
1 year, in the company's annual report
questions.explanation: Article 33 sets 72 hours; if the risk is high, the individuals concerned must also be informed (Article 34).

whyNot.0: Notification is mandatory unless the risk is unlikely.

questions.prompt: Which statements about DLP are correct? (several answers)
choices: It can act on the endpoint, the network and the cloud
It replaces data classification
It relies on the content or the classification label
It can block or only alert
questions.explanation: DLP applies rules based on classification and content; it does not replace classification.

whyNot.1: Good classification makes DLP more accurate; DLP does not replace it.
